msItem.title: A Complaint to the Nightingale, taken out of St. Bonaventure
msItem.author: Henrie Vaux

lg.l: Thou worthy bird, thou gentle Nightingale,
Leave of a while thy wonted songes, I pray;
And lend thine care to this my doleful tale,
And make report of that which I shal say:
Since this my barren Verse is far to base
Before my Sovereign Lord to pleade my case.
For wel I know thy swete melodious throate
Wil never cease with warbling tunes ful hie
To praise our God with many a pleasant note
when senelesse slepe shal close my fainting eie:
And wel I know thou maist ascend by right,
When I pore soule dare scarce direct my sight.
Goe, tel my Love I languish for his love,
Since he in heaven, and I at brinke of hel,
Since he in height of roial throne above,
And I in depth of wreched vale do dwell;
Since he in peace, and I in strife and paine;
Since he in blisse, and I in woe remaine.
Since him I lacke, without whose sight most dere
My soule each day for want of fode doth die;
Since him I lacke, the wel of blisse most clere,
My tired ghost is werie, weake, and drie;
Since him I lacke, my sole an sov’ran weale.
The onely want wherby all joyes do faile.
Goe say I waile that I ne liv’d that day.
My blessed Lord beneath in earth to see,
In Bethlem borne, and porely coucht in hay,
With Shepherdes, and with roial Sages three;
Or in his Circumcision sore to blede,
When Marie wept to see that woful dede.
Ne yet with Simeon old I might embrace
The light, and health, and glorie of man-kind;
Ne yet to AEgyptward with spedie pase
I plide my fete, my Saviour there to find;
Ne yet in midst of learned Doctours found
My hap was soch to heare his sacred sound.
Wold God in Nazareth I might have dwelt,
In growing age to see my Love most dere;
At Jordanes bancke great joy I might have felt,
With John to see the blessed Lambe appere;
The Father's voice to heare from heaven above,
The holie Ghost to see in fourme of Dove.
What comfort wold have bene to heare him teache
With wordes most swete the simple folke each day?
And toyling ev’ry wheare about to preache,
And humbled oft on knees by night to pray?
To yeeld relief for ev’ry sort of paine,
And with his voice to raise the dead againe?
With Magdalen perhaps I might have wette
His fete, and so have washt my soule from blame;
Or with the rest my Lord I hould have mette
At Sion gates triumphing when he came;
With bowes of palme I should have strew’d the strete,
Praising my Saviour with Osanna swete.
Nut o swete feast, o pretious banqwet dere!
Thy secret joyes can not be wel exprest;
Thy mysteries, which holie Angels feare,
With silence to adore I thinke it best;
Save that I nedes must muse at his good hap,
That might have leave to rest in Jesus lap.
Yet more I mourne that I ne felt my part
Of al his paines endured for my sake;
When ful of deadly drede and inward smart
His soule was irke the cuppe of death to take;
And whils’t he praid prostrate upon his face,
The bloudie droppes ranne trickeling down a pace.
Of al his dere Disciples sone forsaken
With battes, with billes, with glaives, and many a light,
Helplesse alone my libertie was taken,
Fast bound, and brought in furious wise by night
To Annas house, where for his answere meke
A boistrous blowe he bare upon his cheke.
Thence drawne and driven to Caiphas hall anone,
Where slaundred foule with many a shamelesse lie
Through witnesse false, where truth appered none,
Guildles, alas, they judge my Life to die;
Blindfold, bespitte, and bounst with spitely blowes
The restlesse night he spent among his foes.
Disposed thinges may live,
Although they pine in paine;
And thinges oft trodden under fete
May once yet rise againe.
The stone which lies ful low,
May be at last ful hie;
And stand on toppe of stately Towre
In sight of ev’ry eie.
The rotes of rotten redes
In swelling seas are sene;
And when each tide hath tos’t his worst
They grow againe ful grene.
I see no sight on earth
But it to chaunge inclines;
And little clowdes do over-cast
The brightest Sunne that shines.
No flower is so fresh
But frost may it deface;
No man so sure in any seate,
But he may lose his place.
Wherefore I stand content,
Though mock against my mind,
To take in woorth this luckelesse lotte,
That is to me assign’d.
